1.pericope_label: Praise ye the Lord, praise ye the Lord from the heavens, praise him in the heights: praise ye him, all his angels: praise ye him, sun and moon: praise him, ye heaven of heavens, and ye waters that be above the heavens

schools.summary: Augustine takes the psalm as a discipline for this life, since the subject of our meditation now should be the praises of God, the everlasting exaltation of the life hereafter being praise, and no one becomes fit for that life who has not practised for it here; our praise is marked by joy and our prayer by groans, and the two seasons of the church year, before and after Easter, signify the tribulation we are in and the rest we hope for, the one kept in fasting and prayer, the other in praises with the fast relaxed.

Calvin sets out the plan of the psalm, which calls on all creatures above and below, beginning with angels and passing to the brute creation and dumb elements, then to men as the appointed heralds of praise, and at the close to the children of Israel as principal witnesses, since the unbelieving are blind to God’s works and dumb to his praises; he adds that Milton imitated the psalm elegantly and put it into the mouths of Adam and Eve as their morning hymn in innocency. Gill makes the sun and moon praise God by doing the work appointed them and by giving men cause to praise him for their light and warmth.

Spurgeon presses the summons, since whoever hears the word is invited, entreated and commanded to magnify the Lord, and those nearest the High and lofty One should lead the song and let their worship fall like a golden shower on men beneath; no place is too high for the praises of the most High, the summit of creation showing his glory as the tops of the highest Alps are tipped with the same sun that gladdens the valleys, and he counts the word praise sounding nine times in the first five verses. Henry admits that he does not find it easy to account for a man on earth exciting angels to praise God, and is content to say that it is God’s glory to have such attendants and much more his glory that he neither needs them nor can be benefited by them, while we are cold and flat and often interrupted in a work they never rest from.

Clarke calls this the most sublime hymn of praise in the whole book, notes that it has no title while one old version attributes it to two prophets, explains that the phrase from the heavens takes in all their inhabitants as the answering phrase does of the earth, expands the heaven of heavens into systems of systems reaching as far beyond the solar system as that reaches beyond the lowest deeps, takes the waters above for clouds and vapours and rain and snow, and states the principle behind addressing things without speech, that every work of God’s hand partakes so much of his perfections that it needs only to be studied to show forth his wisdom.

Keil and Delitzsch ground the call in the might and honour God has bestowed on his people now that they are gathered again out of exile and their city is risen from its ruins, observe that the hymn of the three in the furnace, interpolated in the Greek text of another book, is largely an imitation of this psalm, and note that in the liturgy it bears the name of Laudes. Ellicott allows that some would render the opening as ye of the heavens but prefers the received version on the ground of the parallelism, since heavens and heights, like angels and hosts, are analogous pairs with the larger term placed last; and he says the invocation pauses at the heaven of heavens to gather all the heights together before descending to the earth, explaining the world of water as what the Hebrew cosmology set upon the firmament.

debates: How should the opening phrase be rendered? Ellicott allows that some would make it ye of the heavens but prefers the received version, since heavens and heights, like angels and hosts, are analogous pairs with the larger term placed last.

What is meant by calling on angels to praise God? Henry admits the difficulty and does not resolve it; Calvin asks how zeal like theirs can need exhortation; Spurgeon simply tells them to lead the song.

What are the heaven of heavens and the waters above? Clarke expands them into systems of systems and into clouds and rain and snow; Ellicott explains the water as what the Hebrew cosmology set upon the firmament.
outliers: Calvin notes that Milton imitated this psalm in his poem and gave it to Adam and Eve as their morning hymn in innocency.
Keil and Delitzsch observe that the hymn of the three in the furnace, interpolated in the Greek text of another book, is largely an imitation of this psalm.
Spurgeon counts the word praise sounding nine times in the first five verses, and compares the summit of creation to Alpine peaks tipped with the sun that gladdens the valleys.
themes: a psalm that calls on everything
angels told to lead the song

5.pericope_label: Let them praise the name of the Lord, for he commanded and they were created: he hath also stablished them for ever and ever: praise the Lord from the earth, ye dragons and all deeps: fire and hail, snow and vapours, stormy wind fulfilling his word: mountains and all hills, fruitful trees and all cedars

schools.summary: Henry pauses over our position, since this earth and its atmosphere are the very sediment of the universe and it concerns us to find what reconciles us to a place in it; next to the visit the Son of God once made here he knows nothing better than that even in this dark world God is praised, and as the sun’s rays are darted from heaven and reflected back more weakly, so should the praises of God be, with which this cold and infected world is to be warmed and perfumed.

Gill applies the establishing to the angels, made immortal and confirmed in their happiness; he supplies the histories behind the fire and hail, the lightning that consumed the cities of the plain and the hail that was one of the plagues and slew the Canaanites; and he adds the gold and silver and brass and iron that the hills contain.

Clarke takes the creating word as the utterance of an idea in the infinite mind and reads the establishing as the fixing of the revolutions of the heavenly bodies so exactly that they have never passed the line marked out nor intercepted one another in the vortex of space; he fills the deep with whales and sharks and with whirlpools and ground tides and the flux and reflux of the ocean, holding that everything in its place shows forth the perfections of its Creator; he ranges over the air in all its forms, breeze and gale and whirlwind and tempest and tornado; and he turns geologist on the mountains, taking in hills primitive and secondary and alluvial with their quarries and mines and minerals and exclaiming at the wisdom lavished on the precious stones. Wesley says the heavenly bodies are constant and incorruptible, not changeable like the things below.

Ellicott renders the verb of the sixth verse as making to stand and takes the second clause to say that God has made an ordinance and will not transgress it, rather than that the creatures do not; he says the line anticipates, but only in form, the modern doctrine of the inviolability of natural order, since what makes the law invariable is the faithfulness of God, and cites two prophetic passages supposing a covenant between God and nature; he objects that the received English rendering violates the usage of the verb; he notes that the invocation passes downwards and that the first sound of earthly praise comes from the sea-monsters, following the order of the creation story; and he gives the fullest note of all on the powers of the air, taking the vapours for smoke and finding a possible chiasmus, quoting a modern poet on smoky mountain tops, and calling the summons a fine poetic touch that shows how freely the lyric handles the creation story, since the poet finds a region of life the story passes over.

debates: How should the sixth verse be construed? Ellicott makes God the subject of both verbs, so that he has made an ordinance and will not transgress it, and objects that the received English rendering, which makes the ordinance itself imperishable, violates the usage of the verb.

Does the verse anticipate the fixity of natural law? Ellicott says it does so only in form, since what makes the law invariable is the faithfulness of God rather than any property of nature; Clarke reads it as the exact fixing of the heavenly revolutions.

What are the vapours of the eighth verse? Ellicott takes the word for smoke, answering to the fire as the snow to the hail, while allowing that the driving mists of a storm were also called smoke; Wesley makes them hot exhalations.
outliers: Ellicott calls the summons to the powers of the air a fine poetic touch, since the creation story passes at once from the monsters of the deep to the land while the poet finds another region of life whose wild voices may join the anthem.
Henry calls this earth and its atmosphere the very sediment of the universe, and finds our reconciliation to a place in it partly in the fact that God is praised even here.
Clarke reads the establishing of the heavenly bodies as their never having passed the line marked out for them nor intercepted one another in the vortex of space.
themes: praise reflected from the sediment of the universe
a region of life the story passes over
wind that is only a messenger

10.pericope_label: Beasts and all cattle, creeping things and flying fowl: kings of the earth and all people, princes and all judges of the earth: both young men and maidens, old men and children: let them praise the name of the Lord, for his name alone is excellent: he also exalteth the horn of his people

schools.summary: Gill notes that the beasts wait on God for their food and in their manner praise him for it, observes that the order of creation is kept throughout so that man, made last, is called on last and the chief among men first, and says kings have cause to praise God since promotion comes from him who sets up kings and puts them down; he divides the praise of the young, the men for their strength and the maidens for their beauty, and makes the horn an emblem of power and dominion while reporting the interpretation that finds Christ in it.

Clarke sorts the animals into wild beasts, domestic animals kept for the house and for agriculture, and the whole class of reptiles, which he measures from the boa constrictor that can swallow a royal tiger whole down to a poisonous creature no thicker than a needle and the animals in water that need a microscope, finding in their production and habits a profusion of wisdom that would take ages to exhibit; the structure of birds holds him longest, with the exact mathematical manner in which they swim the air and steer their course. He takes the human ranks in turn, kings as representatives of the Most High, princes as governors of provinces and judges as executing the laws that preserve civil society, and pairs the ends of life as very appropriately united, since the beginning and the conclusion present nearly the same passions and infirmities. He closes with a peroration on a universal chorus in which God loves man wherever found, of whatever colour and in whatever circumstances, so that the lisp of the infant, the shout of the adult and the sigh of the aged ascend as one gratitude-offering. Wesley says the horn commonly denotes strength, victory, glory and felicity.

Ellicott keeps to the arrangement of the tenth verse, the wild set against the domesticated and the creeping things against the birds; he marks the turn to mankind as a change of role, since the whole universe having been summoned, man takes his place as leader of the choir in language framed to include all ranks and nations, of every age and each sex; he corrects excellent to exalted in the thirteenth verse and finds a fine artistic touch in the order of its words; and he renders the last verse as God raising a horn for his people, takes it to imply a victory that gave the first impulse to the song, and answers the charge that the verse narrows a universal anthem into an anti-climax by holding that what is poetically universal remains in fact the covenant privilege of one people.

debates: Does the last verse spoil the psalm? Ellicott reports the charge that it narrows a grand universal anthem into an anti-climax, and answers that what is poetically universal remains in fact the covenant privilege of one people, which he thinks disposes of the objection.

What is the horn that is raised? Ellicott takes it for a victory or the assurance of one, which gave the first impulse to the song; Gill makes it an emblem of power and dominion and reports an interpretation that finds Christ in it; Wesley makes it strength, victory, glory and felicity.

Where does man stand in the psalm? Gill notes that the order of creation is kept, so that man made last is called on last; Ellicott makes him leader of the choir once the rest of the universe has been summoned.
outliers: Clarke measures the class of reptiles from the boa constrictor that can swallow a royal tiger whole to a poisonous creature no thicker than a fine needle.
Clarke ends his commentary on the psalm with a peroration in which God loves man wherever found, of whatever colour, so that the lisp of the infant and the sigh of the aged ascend together.
Clarke calls the young and the old very appropriately united, since the beginning and the conclusion of life present nearly the same passions and infirmities.
themes: a chorus that runs down to the microscope
the mathematics of a bird in flight
man as leader of the choir
the two ends of life paired
a horn raised for one people
